name: Mingei folk craft
summary: A Japanese movement that began in 1926. Yanagi Sōetsu and the potters Hamada Shōji and Kawai Kanjirō praised plain pots by unknown village potters and made new pots of the same kind.

philosophy.core_thesis: The most beautiful pots are the plain tools of daily life that anonymous craftspeople make in large numbers, with local clay and no wish for fame.
design_principles: Use the local clay and the local glaze material of the village, within 10 km of the kiln.
Make strong, useful forms: jars, bottles, bowls and large dishes that can stand daily use.
Throw quickly and with confidence, and do not correct the small errors of the form.
Paint with a wide brush, in 3 to 6 strokes, in iron brown or blue.
Pour or dip the glaze in a few motions, and let it overlap and run.
Use plant-ash, kaki and nuka glazes, fired at about 1250 °C in a wood-fired climbing kiln.
Make the same form many times, and do not sign it as art.
Put the pot into daily use: for tea, rice, pickles and flowers.
anti_patterns: A polished, perfect form that shows an artist's ego
A new design for the sake of difference
A signature that is bigger than the decoration

form.shape: Large jars, bottles, wide bowls, dishes and flower vessels in a thick, heavy and strong shape.
form.profile: A round body with a firm shoulder and a short neck; a jar is wide and low, and a dish has a thick, simple rim.
form.foot_and_rim: A rough, wide foot ring left bare; the rim is thick and has a slight undulation.
form.proportion: Height 15 to 50 cm; the wall is 6 to 12 mm, thick and heavy in the hand.
rules: Make the form strong and for use.
Leave the throwing marks and the finger marks.
Keep the foot bare and rough.

bodies.rule: Use a coarse local clay that is dark and iron-rich after the firing. Do not refine the clay to a fine white body.

methods: brush painting with iron and cobalt
pouring and dipping of the glaze
forming.joins: The pieces are thrown whole; the handles are pulled quickly and added by hand.
forming.details: Visible throwing rings, a rough foot, glaze drips, kiln scars and a loose, rapid brush stroke.

glaze.pattern: A few strokes of iron brown, lines or leaves, under an ash glaze; a plain kaki brown, with a pour of white glaze over it.
glaze.gloss: Matt to satin, 10 to 50 GU; kaki glaze has a deep gloss.
glaze.wear: Ash glaze is hard; the clay body shows on the rim and the foot, and darkens with use.

palette.strategy: A limited range of earth colour: iron brown, rice white, ash green and a little blue.

firing.kiln: A wood-fired climbing kiln of several chambers (noborigama).
processes: wedging and kicking of local clay
throwing and brushwork in a single day
dipping or pouring of the glaze
wood firing for 2 to 3 days to about 1250 °C
firing.scale: A village pottery makes hundreds of pots in each firing; each has a different surface.
firing.signs: Ash deposits and flashes of colour on the shoulder, spur marks, and a rough bare foot.

pieces.form: Wide lidded jar with a kaki glaze and a white pour
Heavy bottle with an ash glaze and iron strokes
Large plate with wax resist leaves and a thick rim
Plain vase with a Shino-type glaze and a rough foot
Wide planter of local clay, left bare and burnished at the rim

positive: kaki brown glaze with white pour
still life on a wooden table, soft daylight

canonical_works.work: Prospectus for the Japanese Folk Crafts Museum
Mashiko stoneware bottle with kaki glaze

Sake bottle by Kawai Kanjirō, Honolulu Museum of Art
Hexagonal dish by Kawai Kanjirō, Honolulu Museum of Art

emotion.target_response: A feeling of plain warmth and trust: the viewer sees a strong, humble pot that has been used, and wants to hold it.

use_cases: a daily-use bowl, jar or bottle in the folk craft style
a museum label on mingei pottery
avoid_when: the brief needs a signed artist piece

modifiers.how: Use a grey stoneware body, a smaller range of forms and a signed seal; keep ash and tenmoku glazes.
Break the symmetry of the thrown form and stack or tear it; keep the stoneware body.
